rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The necklace loss occurred during the Banu al-Mustaliq raid, the same expedition also called al-Muraysiʿ.
rows.anchor: إن ضياع العقد كان في غزاة بني المصطلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalifa b. Khayyat and Abu ʿUmar date the raid to Shaʿban 6 AH; Abu Dharr or Namilah b. ʿAbd Allah is named as Medina's acting governor.
rows.anchor: خليفة بن خياط وأبو عمر بن عبد البر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet surprised Banu al-Mustaliq at al-Muraysiʿ while they were unaware, taking captives; their battle cry was Amit amit.
rows.anchor: وأغار رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم على بني المصطلق وهم غارون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says Banu al-Mustaliq had assembled to attack the Prophet, who went out to meet them after hearing of it.
rows.anchor: إن بني المصطلق جمعوا لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وأرادوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi identifies this expedition account as the occasion that initiated the tayammum dispensation.
rows.anchor: فهذا ما جاء في بدء التيمم والسبب فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some identify the tayammum verse as the one in al-Maʾida; Abu ʿUmar allows either al-Maʾida's ablution verse or this verse.
rows.anchor: على ما يأتي بيانه هناك

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abu ʿUmar says tayammum occurs only in the two Medinan verses in al-Maʾida and al-Nisaʾ.
rows.anchor: ليس التيمم مذكورا في غير هاتين الآيتين وهما مدنيتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Illness is the body's departure from its ordinary, balanced condition; it may be severe or slight.
rows.anchor: المرض عبارة عن خروج البدن عن حد الاعتدال والاعتياد

rows.speaker: الحسن وعطاء
rows.claim: Severe illness that risks death from water or loss of a limb permits tayammum by consensus; al-Hasan and ʿAtaʾ dissent, but al-Qurtubi rejects their view by the no-hardship and no-self-killing verses.
rows.anchor: فهذا يتيمم بإجماع إلا ما روي عن الحسن وعطاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says a wounded, sore-covered, or smallpox patient in janaba who fears dying from bathing may perform tayammum.
rows.anchor: إذا كانت بالرجل الجراحة في سبيل الله أو القروح أو الجدري

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the sick person was granted permission to use clean earth for tayammum.
rows.anchor: رخص للمريض في التيمم بالصعيد

rows.speaker: عمرو بن العاص
rows.claim: ʿAmr b. al-ʿAs performed tayammum when severe cold made bathing dangerous, and the Prophet did not order him to wash or repeat.
rows.anchor: وتيمم عمرو بن العاص لما خاف أن يهلك من شدة البرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Within the Maliki school, even less severe illness permits tayammum when water risks causing, worsening, or prolonging illness; Ibn ʿAtiyya says this is what he recalls as consensus.
rows.anchor: فإن كان يسيرا إلا أنه يخاف معه حدوث علة أو زيادتها

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Al-Baji reports that Qadi Abu al-Hasan and Abu Hanifa permit tayammum for a healthy person fearing a cold or fever, and for a patient fearing worsening illness.
rows.anchor: مثل أن يخاف الصحيح نزلة أو حمى

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: A stricter view attributed to al-Shafiʿi allows tayammum only when death is feared; Qadi Abu al-Hasan also reports this from Malik.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز له التيمم مع وجود الماء إلا أن يخاف التلف

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi argues that worsening illness is uncertain, so it cannot justify abandoning the certain duty to use water.
rows.anchor: قال الشافعي لا يباح التيمم للمريض إلا إذا خاف التلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi answers that if fear of death from cold permits tayammum, fear of illness should also suffice, since both illness and death are harms.
rows.anchor: قد ناقضت فإنك قلت إذا خاف التلف من البرد

rows.speaker: أبو نصر عبد الرحيم القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri gives the sound Shafiʿi position: fear of death or losing a limb permits tayammum, and the sound view also permits it to avoid prolonged illness.
rows.anchor: والمرض الذي يباح له التيمم هو الذي يخاف فيه فوت الروح

rows.speaker: عمرو بن العاص
rows.claim: In the cold Dhat al-Salasil campaign, ʿAmr b. al-ʿAs feared bathing would kill him, used tayammum, and led dawn prayer while junub; the Prophet laughed after hearing his reason.
rows.anchor: احتلمت في ليلة باردة في غزوة ذات السلاسل فأشفقت إن اغتسلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report shows fear, not certainty, suffices; it calls a person who tayammums junub and supports his leading worshippers with ablution, which al-Qurtubi prefers among two Maliki views.
rows.anchor: فدل هذا الحديث على إباحة التيمم مع الخوف لا مع اليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other Maliki view bars a tayammum imam from leading people with ablution because the imam should have the higher ritual rank.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني أنه لا يصلي لأنه أنقص فضيلة من المتوضىء

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: A report from Jabir says a tayammum imam must not lead worshippers who have ablution; al-Daraqutni grades its chain weak.
rows.anchor: روى الدارقطني من حديث جابر بن عبد الله

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Jabir recounts that a companion with a head wound and janaba was told to bathe, died, and the Prophet blamed those who failed to tell him to tayammum and bind the wound, wipe over it, and wash the rest.
rows.anchor: فأصاب رجلا منا حجر فشجه في رأسه ثم احتلم

rows.speaker: الدارقطني
rows.claim: Al-Daraqutni says the Jabir wound report is weak through al-Zubayr b. Khurayq; al-Awzaʿi's Ibn ʿAbbas route is the sounder version, while another route is mursal. Ibn Abi Hatim records a musnad route.
rows.anchor: لم يروه عن عطاء عن جابر غير الزبير بن خريق

rows.speaker: داود
rows.claim: Dawud reads the term sick literally: anyone who can be called ill may use tayammum.
rows.anchor: كل من انطلق عليه اسم المريض فجائز له التيمم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya calls Dawud's view an outlier; scholars mean illness harmed by water, such as smallpox or fever, as in Ibn ʿAbbas's report.
rows.anchor: إنما هو عند علماء الأمة لمن خاف من استعمال الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When water is unavailable, tayammum is allowed on a journey of any length under Malik and most scholars; requiring a prayer-shortening or devotional journey is weak.
rows.anchor: يجوز التيمم بسبب السفر طال أو قصر عند عدم الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars agree tayammum is allowed while travelling, but disagree about residence: Malik, his followers, Abu Hanifa, and Muhammad allow it there too.
rows.anchor: أجمع العلماء على جواز التيمم في السفر

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi and al-Tabari bar tayammum for a healthy resident except when death is feared; they, al-Layth, and al-Tabari require prayer repetition when resident water is absent and time is feared.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز للحاضر الصحيح أن يتيمم إلا أن يخاف التلف

rows.speaker: أبو يوسف وزفر
rows.claim: Abu Yusuf and Zufar prohibit tayammum for residents, whether the reason is illness or fear that prayer time will end.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز التيمم في الحضر لا لمرض ولا لخوف الوقت

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik treats illness and travel as the usual cases where water is absent: residents and healthy people may analogically use tayammum if water is unavailable, obstructed, or time would pass.
rows.anchor: ذكر الله تعالى المرضى والمسافرين في شرط التيمم خرج على الأغلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who exclude healthy residents argue that the text conditioned this concession on illness or travel, like fasting exemption and shortened prayer.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى جعل التيمم رخصة للمريض والمسافر كالفطر وقصر الصلاة

rows.speaker: الحسن وعطاء
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and ʿAtaʾ say the explicit condition of finding no water bars everyone from tayammum when water is available; Abu ʿUmar says this would be sound without the majority view and transmitted reports.
rows.anchor: إنما شرطه الله تعالى مع عدم الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Prophet allowed travelling ʿAmr to use tayammum when bathing risked death, a sick person is even more entitled to it.
rows.anchor: وقد أجاز رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم التيمم لعمرو بن العاص

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: أبو نصر عبد الرحيم القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri reads the toilet clause as covering a resident who lacks water, and says the rare residential case raises disagreement about repeating the prayer.
rows.anchor: يعني المقيم إذا عدم الماء تيمم

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: For a resident who tayammums, the famous and correct Maliki view does not require repeating once water is found; Ibn Habib and Muhammad b. ʿAbd al-Hakam require repetition.
rows.anchor: المشهور من مذهب مالك أنه لا يعيد وهو الصحيح

rows.speaker: أبو الجهيم بن الحارث بن الصمة الأنصاري
rows.claim: Abu al-Juhaym reports that the Prophet delayed answering a man's greeting until he wiped his face and hands on a wall; another route says he lacked ritual purity.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الجهيم بن الحارث بن الصمة الأنصاري

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ghaʾit originally meant a hollow in the land; because people used secluded hollows to relieve themselves, the word came to denote human excretion.
rows.anchor: الغائط أصله ما انخفض من الأرض

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri reads al-ghayt; al-Qurtubi says it may be a lightened form of al-ghayt or a y-for-waw reversal from al-ghawt.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري: «من الغيط» فيحتمل أن يكون

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes aw as wa, making the cause tayammum the minor event itself and supporting its use by residents.
rows.anchor: إن كنتم مرضى أو على سفر وجاء أحد منكم من الغائط

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi prefers aw in its ordinary sense, with ellipsis: illness preventing water use, or travel with no water and a need for it.
rows.anchor: أنها على بابها عند أهل النظر

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ghaʾit covers minor ablution nullifiers; the strongest Maliki classification groups them as loss of reason, customary discharge, and touching.
rows.anchor: يجمع بالمعنى جميع الأحداث الناقضة للطهارة الصغرى

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Maliki nullifiers fall into three kinds; Hanafis count impure bodily emissions regardless of outlet but exclude touching.
rows.anchor: وعلى مذهب أبي حنيفة ما خرج من الجسد من النجاسات

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: الشافعي ومحمد بن عبد الحكم
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi and Muhammad b. ʿAbd al-Hakam count anything from either outlet, even if unusual, and include touching.
rows.anchor: وعلى مذهب الشافعي ومحمد بن عبد الحكم ما خرج من السبيلين

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims agree that fainting, insanity, and intoxication, as losses of reason, require ablution.
rows.anchor: المسلمين أجمعوا على أن من زال عقله بإغماء أو جنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sleep has three positions: it is itself an invalidator, never an invalidator without another event, or a middle case based on its depth or posture.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا في النوم هل هو حدث كسائر الأحداث

rows.speaker: المزني أبو إبراهيم إسماعيل
rows.claim: Al-Muzani treats any amount of sleep as an invalidator; this is implied by Malik's Muwatta wording and by the Safwan report.
rows.anchor: ذهب المزني أبو إبراهيم إسماعيل إلى أنه حدث

rows.speaker: صفوان بن عسال المرادي
rows.claim: Safwan reports the Prophet allowed wiping over the khuffs after urine, stool, or sleep, removing them only for janaba; al-Qurtubi says al-Tirmidhi authenticated the report.
rows.anchor: أتيت صفوان بن عسال المرادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proponents equate sleep with urine and stool because deep sleep overwhelms reason; they also cite Ali's general report that sleep loosens the anal tether and requires ablution.
rows.anchor: والقياس أنه لما كان كثيره وما غلب على العقل منه حدثا

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
rows.claim: Abu Musa regarded sleep as no invalidator at all unless another event occurred; he would sleep under guard and pray on waking, as did ʿUbayda, Saʿid b. al-Musayyab, and al-Awzaʿi in one report.
rows.anchor: فروي عن أبي موسى الأشعري ما يدل على أن النوم عنده ليس بحدث

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik requires ablution after deep, prolonged sleep in any posture; al-Zuhri, Rabiʿa, and al-Awzaʿi in one narration agree.
rows.anchor: وطال نومه على أي حال كان

rows.speaker: أحمد بن حنبل
rows.claim: Ahmad says light sleep does not matter if it neither penetrates nor overwhelms the heart.
rows.anchor: فإن كان النوم خفيفا لا يخامر القلب ولا يغمره

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأصحابه
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and his companions require ablution only for someone sleeping on a side or sitting with weight shifted.
rows.anchor: لا وضوء إلا على من نام مضطجعا أو متوركا

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi says sitting sleep does not invalidate ablution; Ibn Wahb also transmits this from Malik.
rows.anchor: من نام جالسا فلا وضوء عليه ورواه ابن وهب عن مالك

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi considers Malik's well-known position the soundest of these views.
rows.anchor: والصحيح من هذه الأقوال مشهور مذهب مالك

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports that the Prophet delayed ʿIsha while worshippers repeatedly slept and woke, then said only they were waiting for prayer; al-Qurtubi calls it the strongest report by chain and practice.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم شغل عنها ليلة يعني العشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi interprets Malik's and Safwan's references to sleep as heavy sleep that dominates the sleeper, in light of Ibn ʿUmar's report.
rows.anchor: ونوم ثقيل غالب على النفس بدليل هذا الحديث

rows.speaker: وكيع
rows.claim: Wakiʿ's Safwan route says or wind instead of or sleep; Daraqutni says no one else transmits that wording, and Wakiʿ is trustworthy, weakening the use of Safwan as proof that sleep itself invalidates ablution.
rows.anchor: وكيع ثقة إمام أخرج له البخاري ومسلم وغيرهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the Prophet slept prostrating, then said only side-sleep relaxes the joints and requires ablution; al-Daraqutni, Abu Dawud, and Abu ʿUmar call it unsound or munkar.
rows.anchor: تفرد به أبو خالد عن قتادة ولا يصح

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi, al-Tabari, and Dawud require ablution after sleep in any position except sitting, which is unlikely to become deep; this is also reported from Ali, Ibn Masʿud, and Ibn ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وأما قول الشافعي على كل نائم الوضوء إلا على الجالس وحده

rows.speaker: عمرو بن شعيب
rows.claim: ʿAmr b. Shuʿayb transmits a prophetic report distinguishing sitting sleep, which does not require ablution, from lying on one's side, which does.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: عمرو بن شعيب
rows.claim: The report says a person who sleeps sitting does not need ablution, but one who lies down does.
rows.anchor: من نام جالسا فلا وضوء عليه ومن وضع جنبه فعليه الوضوء

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Bukhari reports that a wife of the Prophet in retreat saw blood and yellow discharge beneath her while praying; al-Qurtubi treats it as an abnormal, illness-related discharge.
rows.anchor: اعتكفت مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم امرأة من أزواجه

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Malik does not make this unusual outlet obligatorily invalidate ablution, unlike al-Shafiʿi; this supports Malik's distinction from the Hanafi rule based on impurity alone.
rows.anchor: وإنما هو عرق انقطع فهو مرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, and Ibn ʿAmir read lamastum; Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read lamistum.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three reported meanings are intercourse, physical contact, or a word covering both; most readers treat the two readings as equivalent in sense.
rows.anchor: الأول أن يكون لمستم جامعتم

rows.speaker: محمد بن يزيد
rows.claim: Muhammad b. Yazid says lamastum more naturally means kissing or the like, since each party acts; lamistum means intercourse or touching, where the woman does not act.
rows.anchor: عن محمد بن يزيد أنه قال الأولى في اللغة أن يكون

rows.speaker: عمر وابن مسعود
rows.claim: One view limits mulamasa to hand-touch and says a junub person is not covered by the illness clause, so he must bathe or wait for water; it is reported from ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿud.
rows.anchor: والجنب لا ذكر له إلا مع الماء

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abu ʿUmar says no leading jurist followed ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿud here, likely because reports from ʿAmmar, ʿImran b. Husayn, and Abu Dharr allow a junub person to tayammum.
rows.anchor: لم يقل بقول عمر وعبد الله في هذه المسألة أحد من فقهاء الأمصار

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa takes mulamasa to mean intercourse alone: a junub person may tayammum, but hand-touch and a pleasurable kiss do not invalidate ablution.
rows.anchor: الملامسة هنا مختصة باللمس الذي هو الجماع

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Hanafis cite a Daraqutni report from ʿAisha that the Prophet kissed a wife and prayed without renewing ablution.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قبل بعض نسائه ثم خرج إلى الصلاة

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: When ʿUrwa asked which wife the Prophet kissed, ʿAisha laughed, leaving open that she herself was the one.
rows.anchor: من هي إلا أنت؟ فضحكت

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says intercourse calls for tayammum; hand-touch calls for ablution if pleasure is felt, while touch without desire does not, a view also held by Ahmad and Ishaq.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك: الملامس بالجماع يتيمم

rows.speaker: علي بن زياد
rows.claim: Ali b. Ziyad says touching through a thick garment has no effect, but touching through a thin one requires ablution.
rows.anchor: وإن كان عليها ثوب كثيف فلا شيء عليه

rows.speaker: عبد الملك بن الماجشون
rows.claim: Ibn al-Majishun requires ablution for intentionally touching one's wife by hand for play, whether or not pleasure follows.
rows.anchor: من تعمد مس امرأته بيده لملاعبة فليتوضأ التذ أو لم يلتذ

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو الوليد الباجي
rows.claim: Al-Baji clarifies the Maliki rule: intending pleasure by touching requires ablution whether pleasure actually occurs or not.
rows.anchor: والذي تحقق من مذهب مالك

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Nafiʿ transmits from Malik that erection alone requires neither ablution nor washing the penis unless accompanied by touch or pre-seminal fluid; Abu Ishaq says erection alone breaks ablution, citing the Mudawwana.
rows.anchor: عن مالك أنه لا يوجب وضوءا ولا غسل ذكر حتى يكون معه لمس

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi requires ablution when any part of a man's body contacts a woman's body without a barrier, regardless of desire; this is also attributed to Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Zuhri, and Rabiʿa.
rows.anchor: إذا أفضى الرجل بشيء من بدنه إلى بدن المرأة سواء كان باليد

rows.speaker: الأوزاعي
rows.claim: Al-Awzaʿi says hand-touch invalidates ablution but other bodily contact does not, citing the verse about touching with their hands.
rows.anchor: إذا كان اللمس باليد نقض الطهر وإن كان بغير اليد لم ينقضه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi calls the Maliki position strongest: touch short of intercourse invalidates ablution, as reported from ʿUmar, his son, and Ibn Masʿud and held by most jurists.
rows.anchor: فهذه خمسة مذاهب أسدها مذهب مالك وهو مروي عن عمر وابنه

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi says the verse assigns three clauses to three rulings: janaba, minor impurity, and touch or kissing; treating touch as intercourse would repeat the meaning.
rows.anchor: فصارت ثلاث جمل لثلاثة أحكام

rows.speaker: الدارقطني
rows.claim: The kiss report used by Abu Hanifa is mursal: Daraqutni notes that Habib b. Abi Thabit did not hear from ʿUrwa, as Yahya b. Saʿid says Sufyan al-Thawri maintained.
rows.anchor: حبيبا لم يسمع من عروة شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Malikis accept mursal reports in principle, al-Qurtubi rejects this one because the verse's apparent sense and the Companions' practice oppose it.
rows.anchor: تركناه لظاهر الآية وعمل الصحابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the claim that Ibn ʿAbbas interpreted mulamasa as intercourse, al-Qurtubi notes that ʿUmar, his son, and Ibn Masʿud opposed it.
rows.anchor: قد خالفه الفاروق وابنه وتابعهما عبدالله بن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the reciprocal form mulamasa is said to require two actors, al-Qurtubi answers that both parties can be described as toucher and touched; Arabic also uses reciprocal verbs for one actor.
rows.anchor: الملامسة مقتضاها التقاء البشرتين سواء كان ذلك من واحد أو من اثنين

words: أَوْ جَآءَ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلْغَآئِطِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that the verse pairs the toilet event with janaba does not exclude touch: al-Qurtubi says the word can carry both touch and intercourse and convey both rulings.
rows.anchor: لا نمنع حمل اللفظ على الجماع واللمس

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi's view that uncovered skin-contact with a woman breaks ablution follows the apparent wording, whether he touches her or she touches him.
rows.anchor: من لمس الرجل المرأة ببعض أعضائه لا حائل بينه وبينها

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: In al-Shafiʿi's view, touching hair, teeth, or nails does not break ablution; precaution favors ablution after touching hair.
rows.anchor: وكذلك السن والظفر فإن ذلك مخالف للبشرة

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi says it is good precaution to perform ablution after touching a woman's hair.
rows.anchor: ولو احتاط فتوضأ إذا مس شعرها كان حسنا

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Touching through clothing does not break ablution even with pleasure; direct skin contact counts whether deliberate or forgetful and whether the unrelated woman is alive or dead.
rows.anchor: من فوق الثوب فالتذ بذلك أو لم يلتذ لم يكن عليهما شيء حتى يفضي إلى البشرة

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi has two views on touching a young girl, elderly woman, or unmarriageable female: it breaks ablution under the verse's general wording, or does not because desire is irrelevant to them.
rows.anchor: إذا لمس صبية صغيرة أو عجوزا كبيرة بيده أو واحدة من ذوات محارمه

rows.speaker: المروزي
rows.claim: Al-Marwazi prefers the unrestricted Shafiʿi view because the verse does not condition touch on desire, as also reflected by Companions and most Successors.
rows.anchor: قول الشافعي أشبه بظاهر الكتاب لأن الله عز وجل قال

rows.speaker: المروزي
rows.claim: Al-Marwazi says only Malik and al-Layth require ablution when pleasure comes through clothing; al-Qurtubi adds that Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr also attributes this rule to Ishaq and Ahmad and reports it from other early authorities.
rows.anchor: من مراعاة الشهوة واللذة من فوق الثوب يوجب الوضوء

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A sound report from ʿAisha says the Prophet nudged her feet when they lay before him during prayer; they had no lamps, and Bukhari records the report.
rows.anchor: وإذا قام بسطتهما ثانيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi rejects the objection that the Prophet could not touch ʿAisha through clothing: the report expressly describes him as touching her, and the Sunnah specifies that touch without desire or intent does not invalidate ablution.
rows.anchor: فكان واجبا لظاهر الآية انتقاض وضوء كل ملامس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi says ghamz is pressing with the hand, like feeling a ram to test whether it is fat, not striking someone with a sleeve.
rows.anchor: حقيقة الغمز إنما هو باليد ومنه غمزك الكبش أي تجسه
